items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Johnny Dodds was on the boat with him, wasn’t he?

ctx.x: So you can find evolution in the reed tradition from the role of the clarinet playing arpeggios . . .
That’s what I’m talking about. That was David Jones was the master of that with the mellophone. He done the thing the clarinet players would do. Johnny Dodds was on the boat with him, wasn’t he?
Yeah. Johnny Dodds. Yeah. Baby Dodds.

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: After Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds left him, King Oliver formed an orchestra...

ctx.x: Well, Paul was one of the biggest in New Orleans Jazz.

Yes. Paul left here and joined King Oliver's band at the Plantation. After Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds left him, King Oliver formed an orchestra, a ten-piece orchestra for the Plantation. And that's where Paul joined that band. And that was, like, 1923 or '24. That's the band that King Oliver was taking to New York in ...(?)... ...(?)..., asked for more money, and he couldn't get it, and the man took Duke Ellington instead of King Oliver to go into the Cotton Club. And that was the beginning of Duke's success.
I see another great name which comes up in your genealogy, because Jimmie Noone and your Uncle Paul married two sisters.

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: And all the real wildcats at the left, like Jim and Noom, John of Dodge, Bonnie de Gat was around

ctx.x: Willie Humphrey, the one that's working with Paul now. Earl Humphrey's brother. He impressed me, but he lived uptown and never had a chance much to him. And he's the one that impressed me, I thought he was a master. There were others, like Big Al Lloyd, who was always in the same track in the summer of retirement. He played if he got a chance. I worked with him, I know him at Twy, and Walter DeCoult, four of us at the Bungalow. Out on the Shellback Road, I worked a couple of months out there with them. He was…
